This page corresponds to the exact occupation O*NET/SOC 47-3011.00 "Helpers--Brickmasons, Blockmasons, Stonemasons, and Tile and Marble Setters" (Helpers--Brickmasons, Blockmasons, Stonemasons, and Tile and Marble Setters): help brickmasons, blockmasons, stonemasons, or tile and marble setters by performing duties requiring less skill: using, supplying, or delivering materials and tools, and cleaning the work area and equipment. Official scope text: Help brickmasons, blockmasons, stonemasons, or tile and marble setters by performing duties requiring less skill. Duties include using, supplying, or holding materials or tools, and cleaning work area and equipment. The core tasks listed by O*NET include: mixing mortar, plaster, and grout by hand or with a machine according to standard ratios; cutting materials to the size needed for installation using power saws or tile cutters; locating and supplying materials to masonry workers according to drawings or numbered sequences; cleaning installation surfaces, equipment, tools, work areas, or storage areas using water, chemical solutions, oxygen lances, or polishing machines; and removing damaged tile, brick, or mortar using pliers, hammers, chisels, drills, wire brushes, or wire anchors and cleaning or preparing the base surface. Common job titles include Bricklayer Helper and Mason Tender and Hod Carrier and Masonry Helper and Marble Helper. Fit signals | The work activity importance for U.S. O*NET 47-3011.00 shows: handling and moving objects (85) and performing general physical activities (82) and obtaining information (78) and communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates (75) and processing information (74) and identifying objects, actions, and events (72) and inspecting equipment, structures, or materials (70) are this occupation's most important activities; the work context shows: long periods of standing and bending and lifting and carrying, exposure to dust and cement and chemical solutions is common, mostly working outdoors in all kinds of weather, exposure to hazardous equipment such as lifting and cutting and scaffolding, close collaboration with mentors and colleagues, and constraints from project schedules and process interfaces. If you are willing to work hands-on around materials and tools and the site, can do ratios and cutting and material delivery and cleaning solidly according to the mentor and drawings and processes, and take responsibility for work safety and process quality and site order, this occupation's daily requirements are closer to your way of working.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (47-3011.00, work context and task scope): exposure to hazardous equipment such as lifting and cutting and scaffolding; long periods of standing and bending and lifting and carrying; exposure to dust and cement and chemical solutions is common; exposure to machinery and cutting noise is common; mostly working outdoors in all kinds of weather; often working in narrow or elevated spaces and on scaffolding; exposure to extremely hot or extremely cold temperatures; and relatively serious consequences of error (material waste and personal and structural risk). This occupation deals with blocks and tiles and stone and mortar and temporary site facilities: one improper ratio or mixing, one improper material stacking or surcharge, one inadequate scaffolding or edge protection, or one cutting or hand tool mistake can all cause material waste, rework, personal injury, and schedule and compliance risk. O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone 1-2 (little or no preparation needed to some preparation needed) (below 6.0 (SVP Below 6.0)); the education section on that page shows 58% requiring a high school diploma or equivalent, 24% below a high school diploma, and 12% a post-secondary certificate (the page does not account for the remaining 6%); growth is labeled Decline (-1% or lower). If you find it hard to work amid dust and noise and chemical solutions and outdoor weather and elevated conditions, find it hard to accept a rhythm that changes with the project and processes and weather and possible overtime, or are unwilling to take responsibility for safety and process coordination, you should treat these as real costs.

Taking on judgment | Real fit comes from whether you can do three things at the same time on one task: do the technical work solidly (complete mixing and cutting and material delivery and cleaning and curing according to drawings and mentor instructions and process requirements, producing usable material and work records), keep safety and compliance and boundaries under control (work and keep records according to scaffolding and edge and opening and lifting and machinery and dust and chemical solution and work permit requirements, distinguish publicly shareable information from controlled materials involving the project and suppliers and handle them according to policy, and do not erect or dismantle or operate or handle out of bounds without authorization), and take on definable job responsibility (be responsible for your own ratios and cutting and material delivery and cleaning and records, and refer matters beyond job authorization or involving special operations and major safety matters to the appropriate position or organization according to policy). It is suggested to test this with one verifiable experience (completing an assisted work plan and an explanation of material and work records for a fictitious task sheet, or a review of handling a collapse or fall or cutting anomaly), rather than relying only on the conclusion of an interest questionnaire.

Direct answer | The "Helpers--Brickmasons, Blockmasons, Stonemasons, and Tile and Marble Setters" on this page is the exact occupation O*NET 47-3011.00 (Helpers--Brickmasons, Blockmasons, Stonemasons, and Tile and Marble Setters), and the work can be divided into several categories: first, materials and ratios — mixing mortar, plaster, and grout by hand or with a machine according to standard ratios, and organizing or storing materials and machines and tools and equipment; second, cutting and preparation — cutting materials to the size needed for installation using power saws or tile cutters, and removing damaged tile and brick or mortar using pliers and hammers and chisels and drills and wire brushes and cleaning or preparing the base surface; third, assisting installation — locating and supplying materials to masonry workers according to drawings or numbered sequences, filling joints between brick or tile and removing excess grout, and assisting with surface preparation, installation, repair, or rebuilding; fourth, handling and positioning — moving materials and tools to the installation site by hand or with handling equipment, and moving or positioning materials such as marble using cranes and rigging or carts; fifth, cleaning and finishing — cleaning installation surfaces and equipment and tools and work areas with water and chemical solutions and polishing machines, and applying sealant and repairing surface defects.

The precise 47-3011 occupation assists brickmasons/blockmasons/stonemasons/tile and marble setters with lower-skill tasks of using, supplying, or holding materials and tools and cleaning the site and equipment. The current 15 tasks are all Core: mixing 85, cutting 82, erecting scaffolding 81, supplying materials 79, cleaning 73, grouting 72; the original specific tasks are correctly retained. Activities: handling 86, obtaining information 82, inspection 81, decision making 77, physical activity 76, identifying 75, monitoring 74, communication 69, information processing 54. The precise U.S. BLS 47-3011 typically requires no formal educational credential, no relevant experience, and short-term on-the-job training; the O*NET new-hire education of 58% high school / 24% below high school / 12% post-secondary certificate is a different measure, and the remaining 6% is not guessed. The current O*NET interest scores are Realistic 100, Conventional 39, Social 15, Artistic 10, Investigative 6, Enterprising 0, and the old RC code is not treated as a current score or ability threshold.

The following five steps are the human responsibility points that must be preserved before and after adopting any digital tool or automated data and report generation.

Task and boundaries: the project location and materials and safety boundaries must be determined by the mentor and personnel holding the corresponding experience and authorization, and equipment and systems do not replace on-site and process judgment.

Data and methods: usage and ratio and material and progress data and their sources and calibration must be checked and reviewed by the person, and insufficient or deviating data must be clearly stated, and gaps must not be concealed by system output.

Conclusions and determinations: ratio and cutting and material supply and cleaning and curing conclusions must be made by the person according to drawings and processes and current acceptance standards, and system output must not be used directly as a basis for release or rework or external publication.

Changes and disclosure: materials and ratios and layout and process information disclosure and structural or design changes must be carried out within the scope of authorization and policy, and when a collapse or fall or machinery or exceeding-authorization anomaly is found, operations must be paused and isolated and reported according to policy.

Direct answer | The core risk of this occupation is not "can the materials be mixed and cut well", but four types of failure with heavier consequences: safety and personal failure (dust and cement and chemical solution exposure, heights and scaffolding and falls, lifting and handling and material stacking, cutting and hand tool injuries); quality and rework failure (inadequate ratios or dimensions or material supply or grouting leading to process rework and a second loss); finished product failure (improper cleaning or curing or protection causing damage to finishes and masonry); and record and traceability failure (distorted material and usage data making responsibility impossible to define).

subject.summary: Helpers--Brickmasons, Blockmasons, Stonemasons, and Tile and Marble Setters corresponds to the exact occupation O*NET/SOC 47-3011.00 "Helpers--Brickmasons, Blockmasons, Stonemasons, and Tile and Marble Setters": help brickmasons, blockmasons, stonemasons, or tile and marble setters by performing duties requiring less skill: using, supplying, or delivering materials and tools, and cleaning the work area and equipment. Core tasks include mixing mortar and plaster and grout according to standard ratios, cutting materials with power saws or tile cutters, erecting scaffolding or other installation structures, locating and supplying materials to masonry workers according to drawings or numbered sequences, and cleaning installation surfaces and equipment and tools and work areas with water and chemical solutions and polishing machines; common job titles include Bricklayer Helper and Mason Tender and Hod Carrier and Masonry Helper and Marble Helper. Official scope text: Help brickmasons, blockmasons, stonemasons, or tile and marble setters by performing duties requiring less skill. Duties include using, supplying, or holding materials or tools, and cleaning work area and equipment. Scope note: the U.S. wage and employment and industry data presented by O*NET on the 47-3011.00 page are not marked as taken from a parent or adjacent occupation, and this page labels them faithfully according to this occupation's (47-3011.00) own scope; this occupation is Job Zone 1-2 (little or no preparation needed to some preparation needed) (below 6.0 (SVP Below 6.0)), with 2024—2034 growth of Decline (-1% or lower).
